newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch swine fever spreads as EU inspectors arrive.
newsitem.headline: Dutch swine fever spreads as EU inspectors arrive.

text.p: EU vetinerary inspectors arrived in the Netherlands on Sunday to review Dutch measures to tackle swine fever with the number of cases continuing to rise, the Dutch Farm Ministry said.
On Saturday, two more cases of swine fever came to light, in Heesch and Rijsbergen, both in the southern province of North Brabant, bringing the number of cases discovered so far to 16.
The Dutch Farm Ministry said the slaughter of over 5,000 pigs in the two areas had begun to add to the 30,000 pigs so far culled.

The Rijsbergen discovery, made late in the day, also brought a livestock transport ban, excluding poultry, to a new part of the province. The 10-km (six mile) cordon around the town also scuppered a horse race meeting planned for Monday.
The Dutch Farm Ministry said they could not rule out more discoveries of swine fever being made this week.
"It's quite possible. More tests need to be done," a spokeswoman said.
European Union inspectors arrived on Sunday to assess the Dutch response to the swine fever outbreak.
"They are here for two days to see if the Netherlands has taken the right measures. They will then make a report to the European Commission," the Dutch Farm Ministry spokeswoman said.
On Wednesday, the European Union's Standing Veterinary Committee backed a ban on exports of pigs from seven Dutch districts.
On Tuesday, the U.S. halted imports of Dutch pork products.
A week ago, Poland closed its borders to all imports of Dutch pigs, pork and pork products and Belgium said it would tighten frontier checks.
Last year, the Netherlands exported almost a million tonnes of pigs and pork products, about 60 percent of its production, bringing in around 5.1 billion guilders ($2.7 billion).
Of 14 million pigs in the country, a fifth are in the "Westelijk Peelgebied" area of the southern Netherlands where swine fever has broken out.
Swine fever, last detected in the Netherlands in 1992, is a highly contagious disease, but is not harmful to humans.
